claims.text: Wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by stress-induced local chemical reordering.
Local chemical reordering produces nanoscale intergranular precipitates.
The nanoscale intergranular precipitates impede dislocation motion during sliding.
Impeded dislocation motion reduces plastic deformation and wear.
The initial coating is an as-deposited, chemically homogeneous, disordered single phase.
Simulated local compositional fluctuations can be used to promote or suppress grain-boundary ordering during incremental sliding wear.
High local stresses during sliding trigger atomic rearrangements.
The stress-triggered atomic rearrangements form nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries.
Coatings lacking local reordering have greater dislocation mobility.
Greater dislocation mobility leads to increased wear.
Compositional fluctuations that foster nanoscale ordering will decrease simulated wear rate relative to a homogeneous baseline.
Conditions that do not promote reordering will produce a higher simulated wear rate.
A homogeneous baseline without induced compositional fluctuations will exhibit minimal local ordering under wear.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate-to-high mechanical stress and at temperatures below those causing full phase separation.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies when localized reordering can occur within the accessible simulation timescale.
The magnitude of wear-rate improvement and the reordering threshold depend on strain rate, temperature, local composition, and accessible simulation timescale.
The hypothesis would be falsified if ordered-region formation does not correlate with wear rate or dislocation dynamics under otherwise identical simulated wear conditions.
